newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria expects bank mergers in new reforms.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria expects bank mergers in new reforms.

text.p: A new policy requiring banks operating in Nigeria to increase their capital base nine-fold is expected to trigger mergers in the troubled sector.

"The time has come for small banks to merge in order to meet the minimum requirement of 500 million naira ($6.3 million) capital base," Finance Minister Anthony Ani said when he explained the 1997 budget to journalists this week.
Many industry analysts said mergers was the most likely way to meet the requirement for some of the banks.
"In the final analysis, banks could merge if only to meet the requirement," said Emmanuel Ijewere, president of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN).
The government announced the new minimum capital base at the weekend when the fiscal 1997 budget was unveiled.
It represents a 900 percent increase from the previous minimum level of 50 million naira.
Ani said the previous level was unrealistic. "No where in the world do you capitalise a bank at half a million dollars and we can't be an exception," he said.
Banks that fail to meet the requirement risked outright liquidation, he added.
Analysts said the measure was aimed at ending the distress syndrome that hit the banking sector in the last few years.

"The development is expected to breed a generation of banks that are adequately capitalised and sufficiently strong to compete in the world market," wrote Tony Ndiulor in the independent Guardian newspaper's financial column on Wednesday.
"It is better to have fewer and healthy banks than to have many sick ones," said Mac Tombri, an accountant.
In a bid to restore sanity to the fraud-ridden sector, so-called failed banks tribunalas have jailed scores of bankers and others found to have looted banks through unsecured banks.

Some of the banks that fell into distress because of such fraud were taken over by the central bank and offered for sale to investors willing to recapitalise them but this has so far not yielded any results.
According to the regulatory authorities 48 or 42 percent of the country's 115 commercial and merchant banks are in distress.
Police say about 5.9 billion naira of depositors funds have been lost to bank fraud, although some have been recovered through the failed banks tribunal.
Bankers said none of Nigeria's 17 quoted banks was currently capitalised at the level now required and that collectively they would need 7.34 billion naira to meet the target.
Among the big three First Bank of Nigeria is capitalised at 215 million naira, followed by United Bank for Africa at 200 million and Union Bank of Nigeria at 158 million.
Stockbrokers, however, said it should be easy for banks in their league, which boast of annual turnover in billions of naira, to meet the new capital requirement.
"There is money in circulation. The big banks will have no problem but for small ones mergers in one option," said one.

($ = 79.28 Nigerian Naira)
